tips.title: Counts in the boxes, categories on the branches
tips.body: A frequency tree holds **numbers of people or things** at each node, not probabilities. The branches are labelled with the **category** each count belongs to. That is the whole difference from a probability tree.

tips.title: Each pair of branches adds up to its parent
tips.body: The two counts coming out of a node must **add to the count in that node**. 42 walk and 28 do not, so the boys box says 70. Use it both ways: to **fill a missing box** by subtracting, and to **check** a finished tree.

tips.title: A percentage of a branch fills the next one
tips.body: "60% of the boys walk" fills the branch below the boys box: $0.6 \times 70 = 42$. The rest, $70 - 42 = 28$, fills the other branch. Questions give the tree in words and expect you to translate it.

tips.title: Probability is a count over a count
tips.body: To find a probability from the tree, read off the **count that fits** over the **count you are choosing from**. Choosing from everyone, the bottom is the root. Choosing from the girls, the bottom is the girls box. Simplify at the end.

tips.title: Watch which group you are choosing from
tips.body: "A boy is chosen at random" means the denominator is the **boys** count, 70. "A student who walks is chosen" means the denominator is the **walks** total, 77 — a number that appears **nowhere on the tree** until you add the two walking boxes together.

steps.title: What a frequency tree records
steps.body:
**A frequency tree sorts a group of people or things by two questions in turn, and records how many end up in each place.**

Suppose 120 students are asked whether they are a boy or a girl, and then whether they walk to school. The first question splits 120 into 70 boys and 50 girls. The second splits each of those again: of the 70 boys, 42 walk and 28 do not; of the 50 girls, 35 walk and 15 do not.

**The counts sit in the boxes. The categories sit on the branches.** That is the whole structure, and it is what separates a frequency tree from a probability tree, where the branches carry probabilities and the nodes are empty.

**Every pair of branches adds up to its parent.** $42 + 28 = 70$, $35 + 15 = 50$, and $70 + 50 = 120$. This rule is what makes the tree useful: a box left blank can be **filled by subtraction**, and a finished tree can be **checked** by adding.

**The four end boxes are the four possible combinations**: a boy who walks, a boy who does not, a girl who walks, a girl who does not. Together they account for everyone — $42 + 28 + 35 + 15 = 120$ — which is the second check worth doing.

steps.title: Filling a tree from a description
steps.body:
**Exam questions describe the tree in words and leave boxes blank.** Translating the words is the skill: a total fills the root, a number or a percentage fills one branch, and subtraction fills the other.

Work **from the root outwards**, and finish by checking that the four end boxes add up to the total.

steps.title: Probabilities from the tree
steps.body:
**A probability from a frequency tree is one count over another.** The top is the count that fits what you want; the bottom is the count of the group you are **choosing from**.

The group you are choosing from is the part students get wrong. *A student* means everyone, 120. *A boy* means the boys box, 70. *A student who walks* means all the walkers — a total that is **not on the tree** until you add the two walking boxes.

check.solution: The choice is made **among the girls**, so the bottom is 50: $\frac{35}{50} = \frac{7}{10}$. The other fractions choose from the wrong group.

steps.title: Frequency trees and two-way tables
steps.body:
**The same information fits in a two-way table.** Rows for one question, columns for the other, and totals along the edge:

| | walks | does not walk | total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| boys | 42 | 28 | 70 |
| girls | 35 | 15 | 50 |
| total | 77 | 43 | 120 |

**Every number on the tree is in the table, and the table has three the tree does not show**: the column totals 77 and 43, and they are exactly the totals you need for *a student who walks is chosen*. When a question chooses from a category that sits on the **second** split, the two-way table gives you the denominator directly; on the tree you have to add it up.

**Frequency trees are a first step to probability trees.** Divide each count by its parent and the tree turns into probabilities: the boys branch becomes $\frac{70}{120}$, and the walks branch below it $\frac{42}{70}$. Multiplying along the path, $\frac{70}{120} \times \frac{42}{70} = \frac{42}{120}$, which is P(boy who walks) read straight from the end box. The two trees are two views of the same data.

**Expected frequencies run the other way.** If the probability of an event is known and the experiment is repeated many times, the expected number of times it happens is $\text{probability} \times \text{number of trials}$. A frequency tree built from those expected counts is what spec point P2 means by predicting outcomes.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
All questions use the 120 students: 70 boys, of whom 60% walk; 50 girls, of whom 35 walk.

**Part A.**

1. How many girls are there?
2. How many boys walk?
3. How many boys do not walk?

**Part B.**

4. Draw the complete frequency tree and check the four end boxes add to 120.
5. A student is chosen at random. Find the probability they walk.
6. A boy is chosen at random. Find the probability he walks.

**Part C.**

7. A student who walks is chosen at random. Find the probability they are a girl.
8. Explain why the answer to question 7 is not $\frac{35}{50}$.
9. Draw the two-way table for the same data and say which totals it shows that the tree does not.

For question 7, work out how many students walk in total first.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The denominator is the group the question chooses from, and it is stated in the question.** *A student* is 120. *A boy* is 70. *A student who walks* is 77. Reading that phrase carefully is most of the mark, because the counting afterwards is easy. $\frac{35}{50}$ and $\frac{35}{77}$ use the same box on top and answer different questions.

**A percentage "of the boys" is of the boys box.** Sixty percent of the boys walk means $0.6 \times 70$, not $0.6 \times 120$. The phrase after *of* names the parent box, and a tree filled with $0.6 \times 120 = 72$ boys walking is impossible on sight, since only 70 are boys.

**Totals for the second split are not on the tree.** Walkers are 42 on one side and 35 on the other, and the question that chooses from them needs $42 + 35 = 77$. A two-way table shows that total in its bottom row; a tree does not, and forgetting to add the two boxes is how $\frac{35}{42}$ appears as a wrong answer.

**Check the end boxes.** The four end counts must add to the root, and each pair must add to its parent. A tree that fails either check has an arithmetic error, and one wrong box makes every probability read from it wrong.

**Frequency trees, probability trees and two-way tables are three views of one data set.** Divide each count by its parent and the frequency tree becomes a probability tree; lay the end boxes out in a grid and it becomes a two-way table. Choosing the view that shows the total you need is a grade 9 move — a table when the question chooses from the second split, a tree when it works down a path.

**Expected frequency is probability times trials.** Given $P(\text{walks}) = \frac{77}{120}$, in a different group of 600 students you would expect $\frac{77}{120} \times 600 = 385$ walkers. That is an expectation, not a guarantee, and saying so is correct rather than cautious.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A frequency tree sorts a group by **two questions in turn** and records **how many** land in each place.
- **Counts in the boxes, categories on the branches.** No probabilities on the tree itself.
- **Each pair of branches adds to its parent**: fill a blank box by **subtracting**.
- The four **end boxes** are every combination once, and they add to the **root**.
- A percentage **"of the boys"** is of the **boys box**: $0.6 \times 70 = 42$.
- A probability is **a count over a count**: what fits, over the group **chosen from**.
- *A student*: denominator 120. *A boy*: 70. *A student who walks*: 77.
- Totals on the **second split** — the walkers — are **not on the tree**; add the two boxes.
- $\frac{35}{50}$ is P(walks, given a girl); $\frac{35}{77}$ is P(girl, given a walker). Different questions.
- A **two-way table** holds the same data and shows the second-split totals directly.
- Divide each count by its parent and the tree becomes a **probability tree**.
- **Expected frequency** = probability × number of trials.
- **Check** every finished tree: end boxes add to the root.

not on the tree: add them

questions.prompt: Explain what a frequency tree records, how to complete one from a description that gives a total, a count and a percentage, and how to find a probability from it, including how to decide the denominator.
questions.solution:
A frequency tree sorts a group by **two questions in turn** and records **how many** people end up in each place. Its **boxes hold counts** — numbers of people — and its **branches carry the categories** those counts belong to. For 120 students the first split is by sex, boys or girls, and the second by whether each walks to school, giving four end boxes: boys who walk, boys who do not, girls who walk, girls who do not.

The rule that holds the tree together is that **each pair of branches adds up to its parent box**: the boys who walk plus the boys who do not equal the boys, and boys plus girls equal the total. It follows that the four end boxes add to the root.

To **complete a tree from a description**, work from the root outwards. The **total** fills the root. A **count** given directly — 70 boys — fills its box, and its partner comes by **subtraction**: $120 - 70 = 50$ girls. A **percentage** fills a branch as a percentage **of the parent box**, so "60% of the boys walk" gives $0.6 \times 70 = 42$, and the other branch is $70 - 42 = 28$. The phrase after *of* names the parent: taking 60% of 120 instead would give 72 walking boys out of 70, which is impossible and should be caught at once. Finish by adding the end boxes — $42 + 28 + 35 + 15 = 120$ — as a check.

A **probability from the tree** is one count over another. The top is the count of what you want; the bottom is the count of the **group the choice is made from**, and that group is named in the question. If *a student* is chosen, the choice is from all 120, so P(walks) $= \frac{77}{120}$. If *a boy* is chosen, the choice is from the 70 boys, so P(walks) $= \frac{42}{70} = \frac{3}{5}$. If *a student who walks* is chosen, the choice is from the walkers, so P(girl) $= \frac{35}{77} = \frac{5}{11}$.

That last denominator, 77, illustrates a point worth stating: totals for the **second split** are **not on the tree**. Walkers sit in two end boxes, 42 and 35, on opposite sides, and their total has to be added up before it can be used. Reading $\frac{35}{42}$ or $\frac{35}{50}$ instead comes from taking a single box as the denominator when the question chose from a group spread across two.

Describes filling from the root outwards, using a percentage of the parent and subtraction.
Explains a probability as a count over the group chosen from, with an example of each denominator.
Notes that second-split totals must be added because they are not on the tree.

questions.prompt: 120 students: 70 are boys, 60% of the boys walk to school, and 35 of the girls walk. A student who walks is chosen at random. Find the probability that they are a girl, explain why the answer is not $\frac{35}{50}$, and describe how a two-way table would have made the denominator easier to find.
questions.solution:
First I fill in the counts the question leaves out. Girls: $120 - 70 = 50$. Boys who walk: 60% of the boys is $0.6 \times 70 = 42$, so $70 - 42 = 28$ do not. Girls who walk: 35, so $50 - 35 = 15$ do not. Check: $42 + 28 + 35 + 15 = 120$ ✓.

The question chooses **a student who walks**. So the group being chosen from is the **walkers**, and that is the denominator. Walkers are spread across two end boxes — 42 boys and 35 girls — so the total is

$$42 + 35 = 77$$

Of those 77, the girls are 35. So

$$P(\text{girl} \mid \text{walks}) = \frac{35}{77} = \frac{5}{11}$$

dividing top and bottom by 7.

**Why not $\frac{35}{50}$.** That fraction has the right number on top but the wrong group on the bottom. 50 is the number of **girls**, so $\frac{35}{50}$ answers a different question: *a girl is chosen at random; what is the probability she walks?* It chooses from the girls and asks about walking. The question asked chooses from the **walkers** and asks about being a girl. Both use the same box, the 35 girls who walk, which is why they are easy to confuse — but the denominator is always the group the choice was made from, and the question names it: *a student who walks*.

The two answers are also numerically different, $\frac{7}{10}$ against $\frac{5}{11}$, so it is not a matter of writing the same thing two ways.

**How a two-way table helps.** Laid out with rows for boys and girls and columns for walks and does not walk, the table has a **totals row** along the bottom: 77 walk and 43 do not. The denominator I needed is printed there directly. On the frequency tree, which splits by sex first, the walkers are in two separate boxes on opposite sides and their total appears nowhere — it has to be added up, and forgetting to is how $\frac{35}{42}$ turns up as a wrong answer. Whenever a question chooses from a category on the **second** split, the table shows the denominator and the tree does not, so the table is the better view for that kind of question.

examTechnique.body:
**Counts in the boxes, categories on the branches, and each pair of branches adds to its parent.** Fill blanks by subtraction, take a percentage **of the parent box**, and check the end boxes add to the root.

For a probability, the denominator is the group the question **chooses from**: everyone, one branch, or a second-split total you have to **add up** because it is not on the tree.
examinerErrors: Using 120 as the denominator when a **boy** was chosen.
Using a single box, 42, as the denominator when a **walker** was chosen.
Taking "60% of the boys" as 60% of the **total**.
Leaving a box blank instead of subtracting from its parent.
Not checking that the end boxes add to the root.
Giving $\frac{35}{50}$ for a question that chose from the walkers.
Putting probabilities on the branches of a frequency tree.
Forgetting to simplify a fraction when lowest terms are asked for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer fills the tree from the root outwards, takes each percentage **of its parent box**, and checks the end boxes add to the root before reading anything off. It names the **group chosen from** before writing a fraction, and adds two boxes together when the question chooses from a second-split category. It can say why $\frac{35}{50}$ and $\frac{35}{77}$ answer different questions, and it reaches for a **two-way table** when the denominator it needs is a total the tree does not show.
